activities.anchor: The specific breakdown of 1945–47 had concrete steps
activities.caption: line up the breakdown, earliest first
activities.name: cwBreakdownOrder

config.prompt: From alliance to blocs — order these steps, earliest first:
items: Yalta and Potsdam defer the hard questions with hopeful ambiguities — 'free and unfettered elections' for Poland
the US atomic monopoly is demonstrated at Hiroshima; Truman grows steadily harder
Stalin declares capitalism and communism irreconcilable; Kennan's Long Telegram advises containment
Churchill, in Missouri, names the thing: an iron curtain has descended across the continent
config.why: The breakdown was a sequence, not a moment — by 1947 the language of alliance had been replaced by the language of blocs.

activities.anchor: What followed was a takeover in stages
activities.caption: file each country under its scenario
activities.name: cwSatellitesBuckets

config.prompt: Eastern Europe by 1948 — file each case:

items.label: Poland, Romania and Bulgaria — coalition governments, then rigged elections, fully Stalinist by 1947–48
Czechoslovakia — communists win a plurality in free elections in 1946, then seize total power by force in the Prague coup of February 1948
Yugoslavia — Tito breaks with Stalin in 1948 while staying communist
Finland — accepts limits on its foreign policy but keeps its democracy

config.why: The Red Army was already there, having driven the Wehrmacht back to Berlin at colossal cost — the takeover was differently paced by country, and 'Eastern Europe' was never monolithic.

activities.caption: pair each instrument with what it did
activities.name: cwContainmentMatch

config.prompt: Containment's toolkit — pair each instrument with its work:

pairs.right: $400 million for Greece and Turkey — the moment America made the world's divisions its own business
about $13 billion offered to all of Europe, East included — participation would force a choice
an attack on one is an attack on all — twelve founding members, a standing commitment
Moscow's economic bloc, tying the satellites to the Soviet economy

config.why: Stalin forbade the satellites to join the Marshall Plan, and the economic division of Europe became formal — the architecture of the standoff was complete by 1949.

activities.caption: call the tempo — the airlift's rhythm
activities.name: cwAirliftEstimate

config.prompt: At the Berlin Airlift's peak, cargo planes landed at West Berlin's airfield roughly once every how many seconds?
config.why: Up to one landing every 45 seconds at the peak — nearly 280,000 flights in eleven months, supplying a city whose minimum daily need was on the order of 4,000 tonnes.
config.context: 2.2 million people were held hostage by the blockade; Stalin, unwilling to shoot over supply flights, lifted it in May 1949.

activities.anchor: The system was tested to destruction once
activities.caption: find the faulty line — thirteen days in October
activities.name: cwCubaSpot

config.prompt: One line of this crisis summary is wrong — click it:
lines: The US had placed nuclear missiles in Turkey and Italy, and the CIA-backed Bay of Pigs invasion had failed in 1961.
Khrushchev secretly stationed Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba.
A US reconnaissance plane photographed them.
Kennedy chose an airstrike over a blockade.
Soviet submarine officer Vasili Arkhipov refused to consent to a nuclear launch.
config.correction: Kennedy chose 'quarantine' — a blockade — over an airstrike; the crisis ended with a public deal and a secret one (US missiles out of Turkey).
config.why: Both leaders, badly frightened, then built the arms-control machinery — the 1963 test-ban treaty was its first product.

activities.caption: pair each school with its verdict
activities.name: cwBlameMatch

config.prompt: 'Who was to blame?' — pair each school with its answer:

pairs.right: blames Soviet expansionism — Stalin was a totalitarian who took what his army held
blames American economic expansionism — the open-door world the US was determined to organise
mutual misperception interacting with structure — today's mainstream
ends in levels: individuals, states, and the system

config.why: The opened Soviet archives confirmed much of the orthodox case about Stalin while showing how much of Soviet behaviour was reactive fear — and each step of security built for one side looked like encirclement to the other.

activities.anchor: The empire built in 1945–48 came apart
activities.caption: line up the end, earliest first
activities.name: cwEndOrder

items: Gorbachev takes power intending to save communism with glasnost and perestroika
Poland's Solidarity wins elections; Hungary opens its border to Austria
the Berlin Wall is opened and dismantled by crowds — 9 November 1989
Germany reunifies; the Warsaw Pact dissolves in 1991
the Soviet Union dissolves into fifteen states — December 1991
config.why: The decisive choice was refusal: when Eastern European regimes wobbled in 1989, Gorbachev declined to send tanks — the Brezhnev Doctrine was dead, and the map redrew itself without a shot between the superpowers.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — designed, or lucky?
activities.name: cwDeterrencePredict

config.q: Deterrence held for 46 years. Was that because the system was sound?
choices: Yes — Mutual Assured Destruction was a stable equilibrium that worked as designed
No — it demanded perfect performance forever from fallible institutions: Petrov's 1983 false-alarm call and Able Archer 83 show it was luck-based by design
Yes — SDI frightened the Soviets into never trying
config.why: A deterrence system that survives only while nothing ever goes wrong is, in the phrase historians actually use, luck-based by design — and SDI was never built or deployed; the Soviet collapse is credited mainly to internal stagnation plus Gorbachev's choices.
